name: Emeka Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two surface-mount lines at an electronics plant that makes control boards for heat pumps and boilers. Surface-mount means tiny parts, some smaller than a grain of rice, placed onto the board by pick-and-place machines at thousands an hour, then melted in place in a reflow oven. I set up the jobs, load the reels of parts, watch the inspection camera, and fix the line when it stops. I like it because it's half mechanical and half puzzle.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said puzzle. What kind of puzzles?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Like last week, one board kept failing inspection with a lifted chip on one corner, only on the night shift. Turned out the night crew were loading a reel from a different supplier with slightly thicker parts. I use an AI assistant every day for things like that, I describe the fault and it gives me a list of things to check, and it's saved me hours. I also did an evening course in PLC programming last year, that's the little industrial computers that run the machines, just because I was curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, not magic, and anyone who thought otherwise wasn't using it properly. I'd probably say it in the group chat with my mates from college, who are always arguing about this. I'd be the one saying, calm down, both of you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed but not worried. My job's solid, there are four electronics plants within an hour of here, and I've got money set aside. I'd just keep building skills on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant at work and push for us to use it on more of the setup work, like checking programs before a new job runs. I'd keep putting money into my index fund every month, I've done that since I was 22. Maybe I'd do the next level of the PLC course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe slightly flat, like when a match ends nil-nil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you be disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like seeing what's next. I was looking forward to the line running itself and me doing the clever bits. In the dull version, I'm still the guy who crawls under the oven with a torch when a board falls off the conveyor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work who'd be glad of a plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loads of people. My supervisor, Mr Okafor, has been here thirty years and he's waiting it out. He'd be delighted. I'd be happy for him, honestly.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good tool, not magic, and those who thought otherwise weren't using it properly. In the college group chat I'd tell both sides to calm down.
S0.think: Privately I'd be a little disappointed but not worried. My job is solid, there are four electronics plants nearby and I have money set aside.
S0.do: Keeps using the AI assistant at work and pushes to use it for checking programs before new jobs. Keeps up monthly index fund payments and may take the next level of his PLC course.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly flat, like a goalless draw.
S0.quote: In the dull version, I'm still the guy who crawls under the oven with a torch when a board falls off the conveyor.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka is curious and secure, already learning PLC programming for fun and investing monthly since 22. A plateau disappoints him because he looks forward to more interesting work. He is generous towards older colleagues who would welcome it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we should get on with it sensibly. I'd tell people at work to learn the new kit early, because the ones who do will be fine. I'd also say the government should pay for training, because not everyone can do courses at night like I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it's great for me, probably. Electronics assembly is already mostly machines, so the next step is fewer people and smarter lines. Somebody needs to set those up and fix them, and I'd want that to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the PLC course and do a robotics certificate, about a year part time, paying it myself if the company wouldn't. I'd volunteer to run the trial when the plant brought in automatic reel changers and AI inspection. I'd keep investing, and maybe up it a bit, because the companies making this stuff would do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually quite excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses in your plant if that happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reel loaders and the people who check boards by eye at the rework bench. Joy at the rework bench is incredible with a soldering iron, steadier hands than anyone. A camera doesn't have steady hands, it just doesn't need them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that change how excited you feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I'd want her moved into something like repairs or training, not let go. I'd say that to management, plainly, because they'd listen to me if I was the one setting up the new kit.

S1.say: I'd say it's a big change and we should get on with it sensibly. I'd tell colleagues to learn new kit early and say government should fund training for those who can't study at night.
S1.think: Privately it's probably great for me, since electronics assembly is already mostly machines. Someone needs to set up and fix smarter lines, and I want that to be me.
S1.do: Finishes the PLC course and a year-long part-time robotics certificate, paying himself if needed. Volunteers to trial automatic reel changers and AI inspection and raises his index fund contributions.
S1.quote: A camera doesn't have steady hands, it just doesn't need them.
S1.fieldNote: Emeka sees steady disruption as his opportunity and would help bring automation into his own plant. When pressed about colleagues like Joy, his excitement dimmed a little and he committed to pushing for her redeployment. He expects his influence to grow with his role in the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and we need a plan for people fast, some kind of income support while things settle. I'd say it calmly, because I don't think panic helps anyone. I'd probably share practical stuff online, like what courses are worth doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be okay for money. My index fund would probably go up, since it owns bits of the companies doing the replacing, and I've got no kids and no mortgage. What I'd worry about is everyone else, and what the streets feel like when lots of people suddenly have nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd move some of my savings from cash into the index fund, and keep a year of costs in cash. I'd try to get into one of the firms installing robots in factories, because for those two years they'd be desperate for people who know both the old lines and the new kit. I'd also think about a small side business setting up AI tools for little workshops that can't afford consultants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I feel okay about me, less okay about the world around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the streets. What do you picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger cousins, honestly. They're 19 and 21, one's doing a forklift licence and one's working in a warehouse. I can picture them sitting at home at 3pm with nothing to do and a phone full of angry videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you help them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd bring them onto the installation work with me if I could, or into the side business. And I'd lend them money if it came to that. My mum would make sure of it anyway, she's very clear that family looks after family.

S2.say: I'd say this is huge and we need fast income support for people while things settle. I'd say it calmly and share practical advice online, like which courses are worth doing.
S2.think: Privately I'd be okay for money, with investments likely rising and no kids or mortgage. I'd worry about everyone else and how the streets feel when many people suddenly have nothing to do.
S2.do: Moves part of his savings into an index fund while keeping a year of costs in cash. Seeks a job with a firm installing factory robots and considers a side business setting up AI tools for small workshops.
S2.feel: Uneasy, fine about himself but less so about the world around him.
S2.quote: I can picture them sitting at home at 3pm with nothing to do and a phone full of angry videos.
S2.fieldNote: Emeka is honest that he would likely gain financially from the very change that unsettles everyone else. His worry centres on his young cousins and wider social unrest, not his own income. Family duty, reinforced by his mother, shapes his plans to help them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a clear warning, and companies and governments have no excuse not to plan. I'd tell younger people to learn how the machines work, not just how to use them. I'd keep it practical and not get into the politics too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is close to ideal for me. I'd have time to get qualified, move into automation work and earn well during the years everyone's installing robots. After that, I'd have savings and investments to land on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd finish the robotics certificate and apply to automation integrators, the firms that design and install whole lines. By year two I'd want to be on site commissioning lines, which pays a lot more than I make now. I'd invest a big slice of the extra money and maybe set up the little consulting business on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. The bit that bothers me is that I'd be helping it happen faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tell myself it'd happen anyway, and better that it's done by someone who cares about the people on the line. If someone's going to switch off the old line, I'd rather it was me, because I'd at least say goodbye to the crew. I know that's a bit of a convenient story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. If the robots install themselves by then, I'm out too, just later and richer than most. I'd probably travel for a bit and then find something with people, maybe coaching the kids' football team full time if that's a thing.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a clear warning and companies and governments have no excuse not to plan. I'd tell young people to learn how machines work, not just how to use them.
S3.think: Privately five years is close to ideal for me, with time to qualify and earn well during the installing years. Afterwards I'd have savings and investments to land on.
S3.do: Finishes the robotics certificate in year one and applies to automation integrators, aiming to commission lines by year two for higher pay. Invests much of the extra income and may run a weekend consulting business.
S3.feel: Calm mostly, though bothered that he'd be helping it happen faster.
S3.quote: If someone's going to switch off the old line, I'd rather it was me, because I'd at least say goodbye to the crew.
S3.fieldNote: Emeka sees a clear financial runway in five years and expects to come out ahead. He is uneasy about speeding up the change and calls his own justification a convenient story. His post-2031 picture is vague, ending with coaching youth football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to plan for everyone, so let's actually do it this time. I'd want proper retraining for older workers and changes in schools now. At work, I'd tell people not to panic but not to coast either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think ten years is a full career arc for me in automation, and then something else. I'd be 37 at the end, with real money put aside. It feels more like an opportunity than a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the robotics certificate first, then move into automation engineering in the first two or three years. Later in the decade I'd think about a degree part time, maybe in engineering or something like teaching, so I'm not tied to one industry. I'd keep investing every month, and probably buy a flat around year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit hopeful, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound very sure. What could go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable and lazy. I've seen it with Mr Okafor, who was the clever one once and stopped learning. Ten years is enough time to become the old guy who says it'll never happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself a rule, one new course every year, whatever's going on. My mum would hold me to it, she still asks what I'm studying every time I visit. She left school at 15, so she's very serious about it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to plan for everyone, so let's actually do it this time. I'd want retraining for older workers and changes in schools now, and tell colleagues not to panic but not to coast.
S4.think: Privately ten years is a full career in automation and then something else, ending at 37 with real savings. It feels more like an opportunity than a threat.
S4.do: Takes the robotics certificate, then moves into automation engineering within two or three years. Considers a part-time degree later in the decade, keeps investing monthly and likely buys a flat around year three.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time to become the old guy who says it'll never happen.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years reads to Emeka as an opportunity. His main fear is becoming complacent like an older supervisor, and he guards against it with a course every year. His mother's seriousness about learning is a quiet driver throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, not for me, for my cousins and people like Joy at the rework bench. I'd be fine, and that's the problem, because being fine on your own street isn't the same as the street being fine. What would help is fast income support and free short courses, plus jobs installing the new kit that go to people from the old lines first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd still want to work if I didn't have to. I think I would, actually. I like fixing things too much.

headlineQuote: I'd be fine, and that's the problem, because being fine on your own street isn't the same as the street being fine.
portrait: Emeka Mensah, 27, runs two surface-mount lines at an electronics plant, uses an AI assistant every day and took a PLC programming course out of curiosity. He has invested monthly since 22 and has no children or mortgage. He sees steady disruption and the slower AGI pictures as opportunities to move into automation and earn well, while admitting he would be speeding up the change. Even fast AGI only leaves him uneasy for himself, but worried for his young cousins and colleagues like Joy. His mother's belief in learning and family duty shapes his plans.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, not for himself but for his cousins and colleagues on the old lines.
whatWouldHelp: Fast income support, free short courses, and jobs installing the new kit offered first to people from the old lines.
